overview: This file concerns Japanese news-gathering agencies and their activities and connections in the United States, especially the mid-1930s consolidation of Rengō Tsūshin, Nippon Dempo Tsūshin, and Dōmei Tsūshin. It consists of a 1934 Far Eastern Division memorandum recording Stanley K. Hornbeck’s conversation with Hiroshi Saitō about foreign correspondents, followed by an internal list indexing related reports from 1934–1939. The indexed records trace merger negotiations, links with the Associated Press and United Press, the proposed involvement of the Japan Broadcasting Company, financial obstacles, the establishment of Dōmei, and British concern about its distribution of fabricated news.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum on Japanese news agencies and foreign correspondents
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, U.S. State Department Far Eastern Division
subfiles.about: Hornbeck records a conversation with Hiroshi Saitō concerning Japanese news agencies in the United States and Owen Lattimore’s conception of a correspondent’s work abroad.
subfiles.summary: The brief memorandum notes that Hornbeck discussed Japanese news-gathering agencies operating in the United States with Mr. Saitō. In that connection, he raised an idea expressed by Owen Lattimore in the current issue of Pacific Affairs about the function of a correspondent in a foreign country. The sheet directs the reader to the internally numbered page 3 and cites another decimal-file reference, 711.94/964; the year 1934 is supplied by the accompanying document list and sequence.

subfiles.title: List of papers on Japanese news-gathering agencies
subfiles.about: An internal index summarizes records numbered 17–22 concerning Japanese news-agency consolidation, international press contracts, and Dōmei’s distribution of fabricated news.
subfiles.summary: The list indexes reports sent by Joseph C. Grew between 1934 and 1936 on the proposed consolidation of Rengō Tsūshin and Nippon Dempo Tsūshin, which respectively held contracts with the Associated Press and United Press. It notes a revised plan involving the Japan Broadcasting Company, difficulties financing the purchase of Nippon Dempo, the establishment of a new international agency, and particulars of the eventual Dōmei–Nippon Dempo amalgamation. A 1939 Hornbeck memorandum concerns Dōmei’s intensive circulation of apparently fabricated news and a telephone conversation with the British Ambassador about a reported change in British Far Eastern policy. The final, heavily garbled entry cross-references conversations involving Mr. Eide and a review or document associated with Mr. Fulling.

interest: The file is useful as a compact roadmap to State Department reporting on the creation of Dōmei, showing that officials followed not only the institutional and financial mechanics of Japanese press consolidation but also the agencies’ contractual relationships with major American wire services. The 1939 entry connects that institutional history to propaganda and diplomatic concerns over fabricated news and British policy in East Asia. The Hornbeck–Saitō memorandum also links practical discussion of Japanese news operations to contemporary thinking by Owen Lattimore about the political role of foreign correspondents.
